name: Illusory Correlation
statement: People perceive a relationship between two variables or events even when no real relationship exists in the data they observed.
statementAccent: perceive a relationship between two variables or events even when no real relationship exists
meaning: Illusory correlation is the tendency to overestimate the association between two things (often two groups, or a group and a behaviour) based on distinctive or memorable co-occurrences rather than actual statistical frequency. It commonly drives stereotype formation, since rare negative behaviours from a numerically smaller group stand out and get overcounted.
mechanism: The effect is driven by distinctiveness-based processing and the availability heuristic: unusual pairings of events are more memorable and mentally accessible, so people mistake ease of recall for actual frequency of co-occurrence, even when the true joint frequency is identical across the compared categories.

examples.text: Loren Chapman’s 1967 experiments showed subjects pairs of words and asked how often certain pairings occurred; participants overestimated the frequency of associatively linked pairs such as "bacon-eggs," even though no such bias existed in the presented data.

Chapman and Chapman (1967) found clinicians reported intuitively plausible associations between Draw-a-Person test features and psychiatric symptoms, such as large eyes with paranoia, that did not actually hold in real clinical data.

In Hamilton and Gifford’s 1976 experiment, participants read behaviours of a majority and a minority group with identical proportions of desirable and undesirable acts, yet overestimated undesirable behaviour among the minority: illusory correlation generating a stereotype from neutral information.

whyItMatters: Illusory correlation underlies the formation of stereotypes about minority groups, unfounded belief in projective psychological tests, and superstitions linking unrelated events, making it central to understanding biased social judgement and flawed clinical reasoning.
limits: The strength of the effect depends on the distinctiveness of the co-occurring items; research shows that explicitly educating people about how illusory correlation arises can reduce, though not fully eliminate, its incidence.
misreadings: It should not be confused with the general "correlation is not causation" caveat about real correlations: illusory correlation refers to perceiving a correlation that is not actually present in the observed data at all.
origin: The term was coined by American psychologist Loren J. Chapman in 1967, with the clinical demonstration co-authored with Jean P. Chapman the same year.

sources.text: Illusory correlation, Wikipedia. — Chapman’s 1967 coinage, the word-pair and Draw-a-Person studies, and the availability-heuristic mechanism.
